questions.solutionHtml:
Inhibition of elastase
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) is a protein produced in the liver that plays a crucial role in protecting tissues, particularly the lungs, from damage caused by enzymes released by immune cells.
  • One of the key enzymes that AAT inhibits is elastase.
  • Elastase is an enzyme released by neutrophils and other immune cells that can break down elastin, a protein important for maintaining the elasticity of tissues, including the lung tissue.
  • Deficiency or dysfunction of AAT can lead to uncontrolled elastase activity, resulting in tissue damage, particularly in the lungs, and predisposing individuals to conditions such as emphysema.

questions.stem: What is the function of IL1?
questions.solutionHtml:
Endogenous pyrogen
  • Formerly known as lymphocyte-activating factor (LAF). It augments the activity of many cell types, especially T cells.
  • It is an endogenous pyrogen (EP) induces an increase in acute phase reactants is a heat-stable and pH-stable peptide with a molecular weight of 17.5 kd.
  • Interferons have antiviral property.
  • Erythropoietin stimulates red blood cells production in bone marrow.
  • Tnf-alpha, IL-6, lipopolysacchrideare also pyrogens.

Capsase 1
  • The two inflammatory cytokines activated by Caspase- 1 are excreted from the cell to further induce the inflammatory response in neighbouring cells.
  • Activated Caspase 1 proteolytically cleaves pro IL-1β and pro IL-18 into their active forms, IL-1β and IL-18.
  • Following the inflammatory response, an activated Caspase-1 can induce proptosis, a lytic form of cell death, depending on the signal received as well as the specific inflammasome sensor domain protein that received it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an autosomal recessive disorder?
questions.solutionHtml:
Albinism

Albinism is caused by mutations in one of several genes, and most types are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissues, manifested principally by changes in the skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system. It is caused by an inherited defect in an extracellular glycoprotein called fibrillin-1. 

Autosomal dominant inheritance

  • Familial hypercholesterolemia
  • Hereditary spherocytosis
  • Marfan's syndrome
  • Polycystic kidney disease
  • Huntington disease
  • Neurofibromatosis 

Autosomal recessive inheritance

  • Albinism
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Sickle cell anaemia
  • Phenylketonuria
  • Galactosemia

questions.stem: What is the choice of treatment for idiopathic thrombocytopenia purpura (ITP)?
questions.solutionHtml:
Splenectomy
  • Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) includes two clinical subtypes.
  • Chronic ITP is a relatively common dis-order that tends to affect women between the ages of 20 and 40 years.
  • Acute ITP is a self-limited form seen mostly in children after viral infections.
  • Antibodies directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX complexes can be detected in roughly 80% of cases of chronic ITP.
  • The spleen is an important site of anti-platelet antibody production and the major site of destruction of the IgG-coated platelets.
  • Although splenomegaly is not a feature of uncomplicated chronic ITP, the importance of the spleen in the premature destruction of platelets is proved by the benefits of splenectomy, which normalizes the platelet count and induces a complete remission in more than two-thirds of patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is positive in Follicular lymphoma?
questions.solutionHtml:
Bcl-2
  • A translocation between chromosome 14 and 18 results in the over expression of the bcl-2 gene. As the bcl-2 protein is normally involved in preventing apoptosis, cells with an over expression of this protein are basically immortal. The bcl-2 gene is normally found on chromosome 18, and the translocation moves the gene near to the site of the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer element on chromosome 14.
  • About one-third of diffuse large B  cell  lymphomas  have rearrangements  of  the  BCL6  gene,  located  on  3q27,  and an  even  higher  fraction  of  tumors  have  activating  point mutations  in  the  BCL6  promoter.

questions.stem: What is the cause of intracorpuscular defects in hemolysis?
questions.solutionHtml:
PNH

Acquired mutation of phosphatidyl inositol Glycan complement group A gene(PIGA)

  • Deficient in CD55, CD59, C8 binding protein
  • CD59 prevents activation of alternate pathway
  • Chronic hemolysis without hemoglobinuria is typical
  • Intravascular hemolysis
  • Loss of heme iron can cause IDA
  • Thrombosis is the leading cause of disease related death in individuals with PNH.
  • 5% develop AML.
  • Diagnosis: Flow cytometry
  • Treatment: Immunosuppressant and bone marrow transplant

Hemolytic Anemia

a. Hemolysis Could Be;

  1. Intracorpuscular
  2. Hereditary Defects
  3. Defects in RBC membrane
  4. Enzyme defects
  5. Hemoglobinopathies
  6. Thalassemia Syndromes

b.Acquired Defects

  1. PNH
  2. Extracorpuscular (Areas of sluggish circulation or hypo - oxygenation) Immunohemolytic anemia, Infections, Microangiopathic

Decreased GPIIb/IIIa
  • Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia is an abnormality of the platelets. It is an extremely rare coagulopathy (bleeding disorder due to a blood abnormality), in which the platelets contain defective or low levels of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GPIIb/IIIa), which is a receptor for fibrinogen.
  • Bernard-Soulier syndrome: Absence of the platelet GPIIb-IX-V receptor.
  • TTP: Caused by acquire dor inherited deficiencies of ADAMTS 13, a plasma metalloprotease that cleaves very high molecular weight multimers of vWF. Deficiency of ADAMTS 13 results in abnormally large Vwf multimer that activate platelets.

Bax
  • A family of more than 20 proteins, the prototype of which is Bcl-2, controls the permeability of mitochondria. 
  • In healthy cells, Bcl-2 and the related protein Bcl-xL, which are produced in response to growth factors and other stimuli, maintain the integrity of mitochondrial membranes, in large part by holding two proapoptotic members of the family, Bax and Bak, in check.
  • When cells are deprived of growth factors and survival signals, or are exposed to agents that damage DNA, or accumulate unacceptable amounts of misfolded proteins, a number of sensors are activated.
  • These sensors are called BH3 proteins because they contain the third domain seen in Bcl-family proteins.
  • They in turn shift this delicate, life-sustaining balance in favour of pro-apoptotic Bak and Bax.

questions.stem: Fish mouth appearance of valve in Rheumatic Heart Disease is due to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Calcification & fibrosis
  • Chronic rheumatic  heart  disease is characterized by organization of acute inflammation and subsequent scarring.
  • Aschoff bodies are replaced by fibrous scar so that these lesions are rarely seen in chronic disease.
  • Most characteristically, valve cusps and leaflets become permanently thickened and retracted.
  • Classically, the mitral valves exhibit leaflet thickening,  commissural  fusion  and  shortening, and  thickening  and  fusion of  the  chordae  tendineae.
  • Fibrous bridging across the valvular commissures and calcification create “fishmouth” or “buttonhole” stenoses. Microscopic examination shows neovascularization and diffuse fibrosis that obliterates the normal leaflet architecture.
  • The most important functional consequence of rheumatic heart disease is valvular stenosis and regurgitation.

questions.stem: Which of the following type of necrosis seen in blood vessels due to immune reactions:
questions.solutionHtml:
Fibrinoid
  • Fibrinoid necrosis is a special form of necrosis.
  • It usually occurs in immune reactions in which complexes of antigens and antibodies are deposited in the walls of blood vessels, but it also may occur in severe hypertension.
  • Deposited immune complexes and plasma proteins that leak into the wall of damaged vessels produce a bright pink, amorphous appearance on H&E preparations called fibrinoid (fibrin like) by pathologists. 

Coagulative necrosis

  • Is a form of necrosis in which the under lying tissue architecture is preserved for at least several days after death of cells in the tissue.
  • Coagulative necrosis is characteristic of infarcts (are as of necrosis caused by ischemia) in all solid organs except the brain.

Liquefactive necrosis

  • Liquefactive necrosis is seen in focal bacterial and, occasionally, fungal infections because microbes stimulate rapid accumulation of inflammatory cells, and the enzymes of leukocytes digest (“liquefy”) the tissue. For obscure reasons, hypoxic death of cells within the central nervous system of ten evokes liquefactive necrosis.

questions.stem: Which form of cholesterol is present in gallstones?
questions.solutionHtml:
Crystalline cholesterol monohydrate
  • Gallstones are hardened deposits of digestive fluid that can form in your gallbladder.
  • The most common type of gallstone, called cholesterol gallstone, often appears yellow in color.
  • These gallstones are composed mainly of un dissolved cholesterol.
  • Precipitation of solid cholesterol crystals from supersaturated bile has an essential role in cholesterol gallstone formation.
  • Cholesterol stones account for more than 90% of all gallstones in  Western  industrialized  countries. 
  • Cholesterol  gallstones  usually contain >50% cholesterol monohydrate plus an admixture of calcium salts, bile pigments, proteins, and fatty acids.
  • When bile is concentrated in the gallbladder, it can become supersaturated with these substances, which then precipitate from the solutions microscopic crystals.
  • The crystals are trapped in gallbladder mucus, producing gallbladder sludge.

questions.stem: Most Common Morphological difference between Ulcerative colitis & Crohn’s disease:
questions.solutionHtml:
Diffuse distribution of pseudopolyps

• The most common morphological difference between ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease is Crypt abscess.

• Crypt abscesses, which are collections of inflammatory cells within the crypts of the intestinal glands, are a characteristic finding in ulcerative colitis. They are often seen in the inflamed mucosa and are indicative of active inflammation in the colon.

• Crohn’s disease is characterized by transmural inflammation that can affect any segment of the gastrointestinal tract. Crypt abscess are not seen in Crohn’s disease.
